paras: The shooting of William Curtis was the killing of a Black laborer by Saratoga detective James Sullivan at Saratoga Springs, New York, on August 13, 1905, as officers tried to arrest him. Curtis was accused of beating the Rev. Bernard Schulte and his wife with a pipe at the St. Luke's Episcopal rectory in Mechanicsville the night before; both survived. The case ran nationally as a wire story that led with the assault and gave the police account of the shooting as fact; three Black weeklies reprinted it briefly.

Schulte, a New York curate, had gone to Mechanicsville about two months earlier to supply St. Luke's Episcopal Church while its rector, Dr. Oliver Shaw Newell, was in Europe. Curtis, 32 and a native of New York, had worked for several years as a coal and lumber yard laborer in Saratoga, Mechanicsville and Ballston Spa, and the Sun called him "well known in this section." An Albany report in the New-York Tribune traced a possible motive to the employment of Curtis's wife, who had worked for the Newell family but was not engaged by the Schultes; the Penn's Grove Record called her dismissal the "sole reason."

On Saturday evening, August 12, according to the wire, Curtis asked at the rectory door for a drink of water, struck Schulte with a lead pipe as he turned away, and beat Mrs. Schulte when she came downstairs. The Sun's Saratoga dispatch instead said he "forced an entrance" with an iron pipe and that his "main object was robbery."

Curtis reportedly walked twenty miles to Saratoga, arriving late the next morning. Officers traced him to the Harris tenement near West Congress Street, in the Tribune's account, or to Searing's alley, which the wire called "a negro colony." Accounts of the shooting differ, but all say Sullivan fired and Curtis died; the Tribune said he was hit in the head and died in an ambulance on the way to Saratoga Hospital.

The Schultes were first reported probably fatally injured, but on August 14 physicians said both would probably recover, Mrs. Schulte being the more seriously hurt. By August 26 they had recovered enough to return to their home in New York. No report of an inquest or other official inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

The New York dailies printed their own Saratoga dispatches on August 14, the Tribune under "Negro Killed in Chase" and the Sun under "Negro Burglar Shot Dead," a text the New Haven Union also ran. The Associated Press story from Ballston appeared the same day in papers from Vermont and Connecticut to Alabama, Texas and Utah. Headlines ranged from "Negro Brute" in the Birmingham Age-Herald and "Black Thug Beats Minister and Wife" in the Los Angeles Herald to "Fleeing Prisoner Is Shot" in the Omaha Bee. Over the following week shorter versions ran in news-brief columns, including "Fiendish Crime of Negro" in Western weeklies and a Virginia brief that called Curtis's offense "burglary."

In all of these the assault was the story and the shooting its sequel, told in the officers' terms as resistance to arrest; no white paper found questioned it, and the Penn's Grove Record called Curtis "the Assassin."

The Black press carried the case a week later, on August 19, and only in borrowed form. The Richmond Planet reprinted the wire text almost word for word under "Brutally Attacked by Negro / By Desperado, Whom Officer Killed." The Cleveland Gazette cut it to one sentence without naming Curtis, and the Baltimore Afro-American ran a brief on "William Curtis, colored," whose ending is lost in the scan. None of the three added comment on the shooting or the accusation.

Every version of the shooting came from the police side, and they conflict. The wire said Sullivan had arrested Curtis, who broke away and ran, and that the officer fired once in the air before shooting him through the head, "killing him instantly." The Tribune's dispatch said that when found Curtis "shot at Sullivan, and turned to run," while the Sun's said he "sought to escape and placed his hand on his hip pocket" before the detective fired, describing no arrest.

reader.title: Shooting of William Curtis
bases: A Saratoga detective, James Sullivan, shot and killed William Curtis while trying to arrest him on an assault charge; no crowd or mob is reported (A1, A2, A5).
Two independent New York dispatches (A1, A2) and the Associated Press wire (A5) agree that Sullivan shot Curtis dead at Saratoga on August 13, though they differ on how the shooting happened.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Negro Brute' (Age-Herald), 'Black Thug Beats Minister and Wife' (Los Angeles Herald) and 'Negro Burglar Shot Dead' (Sun) led with the assault and treated the killing as its deserved sequel.
Most papers ran the Ballston wire or briefs from it, saying only that Curtis was killed 'while resisting arrest'.
The Penn's Grove Record headed its feature 'Vengeful Man's Crime' and called Curtis 'the Assassin'.
The Richmond Planet reprinted the wire under 'Brutally Attacked by Negro / By Desperado, Whom Officer Killed', with no comment.
The Cleveland Gazette and Baltimore Afro-American carried one-sentence news briefs without comment.

info: Curtis was shot on Sunday, August 13, 1905; the attack he was accused of took place the evening before, Saturday, August 12 (the Age-Herald says 'last Friday evening').
Saratoga (Saratoga Springs), N.Y.: in the Harris tenement near West Congress Street (Tribune), or in Searing's alley, described as 'a negro colony' (wire).
William Curtis, a Black man ('negro', 'colored') aged 32, born in New York, a coal and lumber yard laborer living in Saratoga.
Accused of beating the Rev. Bernard Schulte and his wife with a lead or iron pipe at the St. Luke's Episcopal rectory in Mechanicsville, and of robbing the rectory.
Detective (or Policeman) James Sullivan of Saratoga, who had trailed Curtis with other officers.
Curtis died of the wound: instantly (wire), soon after (Sun), or in an ambulance on the way to Saratoga Hospital (Tribune). The Schultes, first reported probably fatally hurt, recovered.
